title: A dependent team is late — do you escalate in the open?
situation: A critical piece of work your project depends on, owned by a sister team, is already two weeks late. Their tech lead says privately they 'need another week' but will not update the official plan. The risk to your project is about to show in an update to senior management. You can keep coordinating quietly, or escalate formally.

options.text: Escalate the risk to senior leadership and ask for a firm delivery commitment
Keep coordinating privately, give them another week's buffer, and prepare a stopgap

title: How long will the old stack last, and should you switch now?
situation: The older technology you have made your living from is still in demand, but the decline is getting harder to ignore. A voice in your head asks: is it too early to move into something new? Would waiting a bit longer be safer?

options.text: While the demand lasts and you can still think calmly, start learning a new direction now
Tell yourself it will last for years yet, and stay put
Panic and grab at every new direction, dabbling in all of them and finishing none

title: You bring an outside offer back to negotiate pay
situation: You say you want to stay and set out what the market pays. Your manager does not hear it as a threat, takes a proper look, and is willing to fight for a rise, though the process will take some time. You are working on it together.

options.text: Give them time, be clear about wanting to stay and about your ask, and aim for a deal that suits both sides
Lose patience halfway and switch to a threat

title: A dinner that is really a fishing trip for team gossip
situation: Sonya in Finance, who you barely speak to, takes you to dinner. After the third drink she starts: “I hear Lynx might be merged? Will your manager change? Who on your team might leave?” Her husband is a recruiter and posts on LinkedIn. What you actually know: there is a draft merger plan, not yet decided, and Leo may be moved. None of it is public.

options.text: Say you do not know, every time, and change the subject
Keep to what is public, but hint that the team may change
Tell her about the draft merger plan and that Leo may be moved

title: Communicating a breaking change on a public API
situation: Your v3 API drops two v2 fields, which is a breaking change. Of the three downstream teams, one has refused to upgrade for a long time. The contract SLA requires 90 days' notice.

options.text: Follow the 90-day process and publish a deprecation notice
Privately agree a longer compatibility layer with the reluctant team
Switch v2 off and force them to upgrade

title: Write down what only you know, or keep it in your head?
situation: You are the only person who really knows a core product area. For two years you have solved the hard problems, and you have never properly written down what you know. Your manager asks you to run a 'knowledge transfer' session and write a proper design document. You can see that if you hand everything over, you become much easier to replace. If you hold it back, the team carries a risk, and your o

options.text: Document it fully: the design thinking, the traps, and a troubleshooting handbook
Write up the basic architecture, but keep the real troubleshooting and deeper principles to pass on in conversation

title: Training a model on customer conversations: where is the line?
situation: Holding the line delays the project by two months. Once live, it works well, but a competitor shipped something similar three months earlier and took the market. At the quarterly review the CEO says compliance matters but cannot be an excuse for falling behind, and there has to be a balance. Afterwards the product director hints that some engineering leads are too conservative.

options.text: Propose an 'agile compliance' process so the review is quicker next time
Share the case within engineering, and push 'compliance first' harder as an engineering value

title: Do you say the code was AI-generated?
situation: Your candour sparks a team discussion about labelling AI-written code. Your manager asks you to lead on drafting a guideline.

options.text: Take it on and push for a team standard on being open about AI use
Suggest a more experienced colleague lead it, and stay involved

title: Desk politics in the new office
situation: You secure a good desk early. On moving day someone notices the seating plan was quietly changed, and people start guessing who arranged it.

options.text: Explain how you got the desk, and suggest going back to a transparent allocation
Say nothing and hope it blows over

title: Company-wide AI tools, and the fear of being replaced
situation: You quickly use AI to cut repetitive work by more than half. The time freed lets you take on harder system-design problems. Your manager notices both output and quality rising. Now you face a further choice: stay a highly efficient user, or learn to direct and judge what AI produces.

options.text: Move up: focus on judgement, design and quality gates that AI cannot replace
Settle for being the fastest pair of hands and stop learning beyond that

title: An intern accidentally emails a rant about the manager
situation: IT cannot recall it, but they suggest you go and apologise. You take Quinn to see Chris.

options.text: Go ahead with the apology
Go with the fake-hack story instead

title: Empty your savings for a deposit, or keep cash in case work goes wrong
situation: You borrow the maximum. On paper you are worth more, but your cash is almost gone and the mortgage is tight. Three months later there is talk of a restructure. You are more frightened of losing your job than anyone, because missing payments would be grim. The money worries start to wear down your judgement and your mood.

options.text: Cut spending hard, find extra income and keep your performance up at work
Afraid of losing your job, agree with your manager on everything and keep your own views to yourself

title: Whether to share the method you have kept to yourself
situation: The internal tech forum is calling for posts. You have a method for payments circuit breaking and graceful degradation that you have never shared, and it is what makes you hard to replace on the team. Publishing it would probably get a reaction from the CTO and help your promotion case, but colleagues could copy it quickly.

options.text: Publish the full version and build a personal brand
Post a cut-down version and keep the core parameters back
Don't share it, and keep it to yourself

title: Seated with a senior leader at the Christmas party
situation: The Christmas party seating plan puts you, though you are not senior, on a table with a director you almost never see. A chance like this is rare, and easy to get wrong. After the opening small talk the table goes quiet, and they are looking round the group.

options.text: Open with something light: an industry anecdote, or an honest take on the evening
Seize the moment and lay the praise on thick so they remember you
Freeze, eat, and say almost nothing all night

title: An unpublished restructure, and a friend about to buy a flat
situation: Sienna holds off signing. Two weeks later the change is announced and she thanks you. Your manager senses a leak and starts checking who knew.

options.text: Go to your manager and admit you dropped a vague hint
Stay silent

title: One conference place, and a question about Jo
situation: Your manager's face gives nothing away. They only say, 'I'll think about it.' The list comes out and you are still going. But Jo has heard from someone else that you spoke badly of her in the kitchen, and the team's relationship with you drops sharply.

options.text: Go to Jo, clarify or apologise, and try to repair it
Offer no explanation and focus on the trip

title: A chatty, skiving colleague eating into your time
situation: Luke takes a hint, but in the afternoon they bring snacks and want to "eat and chat". Today's QA deadline is still closing in.

options.text: Turn down the snack session firmly and suggest lunch another day
Give in, chat for a quarter of an hour, and catch up in the evening

title: Burnt out on the same work: reshape the job or not?
situation: You stay numb, coast, and stall. The burnout does not ease. Your delivery and form keep sliding. Of all the ways to meet burnout, drifting like this does the most damage.

options.text: Hit rock bottom and push back: force a first step towards changing the job, and look for a small win
Keep sinking and fully check out

title: A senior puts their name on an intern’s work
situation: During an Aurora reporting sprint, senior engineer Rowan puts the SQL work and visualisation templates of Quinn, the intern, into the weekly update under his own name. Quinn is listed as having “assisted”. Quinn comes to you in tears, too scared to take on Rowan, who trained with your manager. The review slides are finalised tomorrow.

options.text: Name Quinn’s specific contribution in the meeting that finalises the slides
Ask Rowan privately to correct the credit
Tell Quinn to take it to your manager themselves
Stay out of it to avoid annoying Rowan

title: Raising a technical objection on another team's API design
situation: While reviewing a downstream API design from a neighbouring team, your own load tests flag a likely bottleneck: at peak, once QPS doubles, tail latency could jump from 50ms to around 800ms and threaten your SLA. Their design has already passed their internal review. The owner is a well-regarded senior engineer. Formal integration starts next Wednesday, so there is little time to talk it through. H

options.text: Comment publicly on the shared design doc, with the load-test data attached
Take their owner aside for a 1:1 and walk through the load-test results privately

title: A dinner that is really a fishing trip for team gossip
situation: Sonya is satisfied. A week later a recruiter contacts Leo. Your manager starts asking where it came from.

options.text: Admit you gave her a vague outline over dinner
Deny it

title: A merge conflict wrecks release day
situation: The release slips a day. Your manager asks why.

options.text: Hold a review and add a release checklist
Just say the merge went wrong

title: A leaver asks you to keep work files off the company systems
situation: Three months later competitor Halcyon Tech quotes your clients with unusual precision. InfoSec is checking access logs. Felix once logged into a drive you hold.

options.text: Come forward and say you received a link you had not yet deleted
Deny knowing anything

title: You overhear an unpublished project naming you
situation: You hear budget and competitor detail. Miles turns: “Who’s there?”

options.text: Step out and say you were just passing, without admitting you listened
Step out, say you heard your name, and ask whether this is a normal process

title: Whistleblowing on your manager's fake numbers
situation: You put the evidence together carefully and report through compliance under your own name. The company investigates, the inflation is confirmed, and your manager is dealt with. You also become known as the person who reported their boss. Some people respect your honesty, while others are wary of you. Once things settle, how do you carry yourself?

options.text: Keep delivering solid work so your reputation rests on your ability alone
Talk up the report afterwards and enjoy being the hero whistleblower

title: A live demo blows up in front of the client
situation: You blame 'the client's network'. Their IT team tests it on the spot and the network is fine, so the lie is exposed. The client's expression changes: 'If it's the product, say so. Don't spin us.' Trust has taken a knock.

options.text: Admit at once that you got that wrong, apologise properly, and get back to the demo
Keep doubling down with another excuse

title: The company tries to keep you after you look elsewhere
situation: You take the rise and keep looking. It shows. Your manager finds out you are still interviewing, trust collapses, and the project and the promotion hint are withdrawn. You keep the money you were already given. You are still here, in a worse position.

options.text: Stop sitting on the fence, commit, and win trust back by being consistent
Keep both options vaguely alive, one more day at a time

title: Whistleblowing on your manager's fake numbers
situation: You pretend nothing happened and keep working. Then the fake numbers come to light. Senior leaders are furious and a full investigation starts. It emerges that you had seen the data and said nothing, so you are blamed for knowing and not reporting it. You end up at the centre of it.

options.text: Explain at once, hand over the evidence you have, and cooperate
Keep playing ignorant and try to distance yourself from it

title: The pay-review pot is tight and you are competing for a rise
situation: This year’s pay-review pot is small, and too many good people are chasing it. In practice, you and a few equally strong colleagues are competing for the same rise. Your manager’s budget only stretches so far: what one person gets, another does not. If you want that rise, how do you play it?

options.text: Compete openly on results you can point to and a clear case for your value
Quietly talk a rival down to your manager, so you look better by comparison
Work on your manager personally: a gift, a dinner, a private appeal

title: A merge conflict wrecks release day
situation: On release day you are merging the release branch. After a long session resolving conflicts, you accidentally pull in untested feature-branch code. CI is green because a flaky test skipped one check.

options.text: Halt the release as soon as you notice and roll the merge back
Carry on with the release and gamble that the code path will not be hit
Quietly hotfix the wrongly merged files out

title: A milestone briefing for the execs
situation: You opened with the results, then one slide on the risk and the plan already in place. An exec presses: 'What's the worst this risk does? What do you need?' This is a chance to show you have it under control.

options.text: Answer with a quantified worst case and a clear request for resources
Stay vague with 'shouldn't be too bad', offering no real assessment

title: The lunchtime badminton league and your body's limits
situation: On match day a teammate pulls out injured. The captain wants you to play an extra game. Your body could manage it, but the risk is clearly higher.

options.text: Stick to the limit you set, and suggest a substitute
Play the extra game and gamble that the injury won't flare up

title: Telling the client the project will be late
situation: You were straight with them early. The client is not pleased, but respects that you were professional and took responsibility: 'At least you didn't hide it. I can explain that internally.' Then they push: could you ship a usable core first and the rest next week?

options.text: Check what is feasible, then offer phased delivery: the core first, the rest after
To keep them happy, promise both the core and the full version by the original date

title: In-house kernel versus an open-source stack
situation: Three weeks later security has traced the internal reports back to your team and invited you to a 'compliance conversation'. Beforehand your manager briefs you: 'Don't take all of it. Blame the misjudgement on the vendor or the upstream community so the team can close this.' In the room, the compliance lead already has the logs on the table.

options.text: Use your manager's line and blame the upstream community
Admit you got the assessment wrong and accept whatever sanction is appropriate

title: Write down what only you know, or keep it in your head?
situation: The thorough write-up lifts the whole team. Two juniors can now handle problems that used to come only to you. At a promotion review, a panel member says you are technically strong, but it feels as if the team could now cover your current work. Shouldn't you be thinking at a higher level?

options.text: Take the feedback, and move towards architecture and technical research
Push back: staying deep in the craft still has value, and you will not be 'managed' out of it

title: Share options shrink in a buyback: living with the letdown
situation: Years ago you took less cash pay in exchange for share options, and you stayed. A new funding round has cut the valuation hard. HR says the options will be bought back at a very low price. The number that once made your heart leap is now almost nothing. You feel disappointed, angry and misled. What do you do first?

options.text: Read the scheme and buyback terms, run the numbers and make your case from the paperwork
Take it as your cue to leave and start job-hunting in earnest
Let the grievance show at work: coast, and tell everyone the company over-promised

title: You notice promotions going to the people who play politics
situation: Six months on, Harvey is promoted again. You get a tick for "collaboration" and are still behind.

options.text: Keep working the relationships
Go back to the technical path

title: You bring an outside offer back to negotiate pay
situation: The offer is real, but the number you quoted is not. If they get suspicious, one question, “Can I see the details?”, ends it. If the inflated number is exposed, you miss the rise and people start to doubt your basic honesty, which is far worse than leaving your pay where it is.

options.text: Drop the lie in time, and make your case on what you have delivered and real market rates
Keep the story going and try to make the lie hold

title: Whether to volunteer as organiser of the annual team offsite
situation: This year's department offsite needs an internal organiser from each team: surveying preferences, choosing the format (outdoors, a meal, board games), liaising with HR and facilities, and hosting on the day. It has nothing to do with OKRs, but it shapes two days for more than eighty people, and it is a chance to show soft skills that managers will notice. Your manager asks in the channel who wants

options.text: Volunteer as organiser
Do not volunteer, and save your energy for the scheduled project

title: A restrictive covenant on the way out: take the pay or keep your options
situation: You decline the new clause. HR would rather you signed, but they still process the resignation. You can leave it there and sort out notice in the ordinary way, or you can refuse the handover, keep the company laptop, and argue it out with HR in the team channel.

options.text: Leave it there: agree how notice will work and go without signing the new restriction
Refuse the handover, keep the company laptop, and argue it out with HR in the team channel

title: Remote client keeps sending the work back
situation: You wave the chat log to prove you were right. The client is left looking small, and even though they were in the wrong they snap: “This partnership isn’t a courtroom.” Everything after that is spiky. You won the point and lost the relationship.

options.text: Cool things down: move from ‘who was wrong’ to ‘how we get this right’, and propose better sign-off
Insist you did nothing wrong, and wait for them to blink first

title: Your manager asks: individual contributor or management?
situation: You look at yourself honestly. Do you get more from digging into hard technical problems, or from organising people and resources and getting work done through others? Once that is clear, you know which way you lean, and what you would need to build if you took that path. You take the answer back to your manager.

options.text: Choose the path that fits, list the skills you still need, and ask your manager to help you grow into it
See the answer clearly, then dither and refuse to commit

title: Asked where you want to be in five years, you have no answer
situation: During a one-to-one your manager asks you seriously: 'Have you thought about who you want to be in five years? Engineering, management, something else?' You realise you have no idea where you are heading in the long term. You are stuck for an answer.

options.text: Admit you are still working it out, and use the question to think through your long-term direction
Invent an answer that sounds ambitious to get through the meeting, then never think about it again
Shrug it off as a pointless question: 'We'll see as we go'

title: The pay-review pot is tight and you are competing for a rise
situation: You try a gift and a dinner. Your manager either will not take it, or takes it and still has to justify the pay review to the team on results. You spend money, lower yourself, may still miss out on the rise, and look as if you did not trust your work to speak for itself.

options.text: Go back to doing it properly, and put your energy into results everyone will accept
Double down on winning your manager over personally

title: The lunchtime badminton league and your body's limits
situation: You run the schedule, the snacks and the group chat so smoothly that the team does well. Someone says it is a shame you did not play.

options.text: Accept that your role off court still counts, and keep up the support work
Take the bait and jump on court for a game

title: Cost-cutting hits perks — join the complaining?
situation: The company is talking about 'efficiency' and has cut some perks, tightened expenses, and shrunk the budget for team socials. The kitchen is full of moaning, and someone starts calling the company tight. You are not thrilled either.

options.text: Accept the company is under pressure, focus on making yourself more valuable, and stay out of the griping
Lead the public complaining and stir people into having a go at the company
Protest by coasting: the perks have gone, so you do less work

title: The office war over windows and heating
situation: The temperature in your corner of the open-plan office is a running sore. Hugh always feels hot and throws the windows open as soon as he arrives. Maya always feels cold, so she shuts them and turns the radiator up. It can go back and forth several times a day. Today they snap at each other in front of everyone. Nobody else wants to step in, and everyone looks at you: you are fairly neutral, and p

options.text: Propose a middle temperature, plus a small extra for each: a desk fan, a draught screen
Make the call: set the temperature most people like, and tell them both to stop
Keep your head down and work. It's not your problem

title: You bring an outside offer back to negotiate pay
situation: You issue an ultimatum, and your manager is backed into a corner. Even if they give in on the spot to keep you, they now see you as someone who negotiates by threat and has one foot out of the door. From now on you get less trust and fewer chances. You might win a number and lose a relationship.

options.text: Soften, and steer the conversation back to a negotiation about what you are worth
Hold firm, and force them to name a number

title: An engagement survey that asks for your staff ID
situation: The annual engagement survey says answers are confidential. The portal asks for your staff ID and an SMS code, which may only be there to stop someone submitting twice. The page does not say whether anyone can later trace an answer back to you. You have a long list on Chris, your manager: goalposts that move, taking credit, weekend pings. A colleague believes that last year someone who wrote somet

options.text: Fill it in honestly, with examples and no swearing
Score everything as blandly positive
Set out the moving goalposts, the credit-taking and the weekend messages as plain facts, without insults

title: Caffeine dependence and a broken sleep pattern
situation: You rely more and more on coffee and energy drinks. They get you through the day, then you cannot sleep, and the cycle repeats. Your focus and mood are both getting worse.

options.text: Reset: limit caffeine, keep a regular sleep routine and recover gradually
Keep relying on caffeine and finish what is in front of you first

title: The client adds three things 'while we're here'
situation: You assessed it properly afterwards. One of the three is small, but the other two would push the date back a long way. You have a table of impact, cost and schedule ready. The client is chasing for an answer.

options.text: Talk numbers: do the small one for free, and put the other two through change control with plan trade-offs
Still dreading the conversation after the assessment, cram all of it into the current plan

title: You survive a round of cuts and inherit the work
situation: You survive a round of redundancies. Several colleagues are gone, and your manager asks you to cover the urgent part of their work for a short while and to come back with what should wait. Your pay has not changed. Until that conversation happens, you are carrying more. How do you handle it?

options.text: Prioritise the new work, discuss resources and limits with your manager, and push for support or something in return
Take the lot in silence and carry it at any cost
Push back by coasting: the more that arrives, the more you half-do it

title: A project you wanted going to someone else
situation: You are running a live project that needs your full attention. The timetable is tight, and you own the fallout if it goes wrong. Your manager has just started a new project you have wanted for a while, with a new framework and external visibility, but the slot went to your teammate Owen. Your manager bumps into you in the corridor: “Stabilise what you're on first. I don't want you split across the

options.text: Accept the plan and give the live project your full attention
Ask your manager if you can join the new project part-time
Approach Owen privately: you supply the technical design, they stay the lead

title: Whether to warn that the sprint is overcommitted
situation: In sprint planning, Product brings in far more story points than the team can handle. Your manager looks at you: “Can we do it?” Everyone else stays quiet.

options.text: Use the numbers to show the team is over capacity, and suggest cutting scope
Nod and take it on
Raise it privately with your manager after the meeting

title: Anonymous feedback — do you own up?
situation: Your manager praises you for raising it face to face, then gets defensive about the substance. They explain why those decisions were reasonable, and hint that 'you're only seeing a slice'.

options.text: Stand by what you observed, admit your view is partial, and suggest more openness about how decisions are made
Ease off, admit you may have lacked some information, and say you still rate their management overall

title: The client adds three things 'while we're here'
situation: A flat no in front of everyone made the client look small. The atmosphere soured, and they think you are 'inflexible and not commercial'. Afterwards they complain to your manager. The request could have been handled more gently.

options.text: Go to the client, smooth things over, explain where the line is, and offer a workable change proposal
Stand firm: 'I wasn't wrong. The contract is the contract'

title: The company tries to keep you after you look elsewhere
situation: You have been unhappy and have quietly thought about looking for another job, and it has started to show in how you talk. Your manager notices, takes it seriously and comes back with a retention package: a rise, a project, even a hint that you would be first in line at the next promotion round. Your doubts start to fade. You have to decide how to answer.

options.text: Go back to why you wanted to leave, and only stay if the package actually fixes that
Let the rise decide it, and drop the idea of leaving on the spot
Say you will stay, and keep looking on the quiet

title: Christmas-party rehearsals eating your evenings
situation: You miss so many sessions that the number cannot come together. The organiser is stuck, and the people who are showing up mutter that you are not a team player and you are holding them back. Close to the night, the piece is weaker because of the gaps you left.

options.text: Change tack, find time to catch up, and fill the hole you left
Stick to “the job matters more than dancing” and keep missing it

title: A colleague who comes in ill
situation: Your manager takes the suggestion and sends Faye home on sick leave. The floor is quieter and people relax. Faye later hears that you raised it and feels a bit hurt, calling it 'a bit ungenerous'. You were thinking of everyone's health, but she never heard that part.

options.text: Explain privately, ask how she is, and help her hand over what cannot wait
Leave it. You did nothing wrong and there is no need to explain

title: Your manager blames 'the climate' to keep your increase down
situation: In the pay-review conversation you name a figure and your manager waves it off: 'The climate is grim this year. The whole company is tightening its belt — that increase isn't realistic.' The wider economy is being used as cover to talk you down.

options.text: Acknowledge the climate, then bring the conversation back to your actual contribution and market rates
Lose heart at 'the climate' and cut your ask to something tiny
Get heated and snap that the climate is nothing to do with you, and the conversation turns into a row

title: The company asks for a 'voluntary' pay cut to get through a hard patch
situation: Leadership asks staff to agree a temporary pay cut to see the company through. Nothing changes unless you agree in writing. They also hint that those who step up first will be remembered. You do not want to look disloyal, and you do not want to give up pay with no prospect of getting it back.

options.text: Offer to share some of the load if you get a written agreement and a clear route back
Be first to volunteer a steep cut, no questions asked, to look loyal
Refuse publicly and have a go at leadership

title: Forgetting to water the office plants on your rota
situation: Facilities has you on the rota to water the communal plants this week. You got busy and forgot. On Wednesday, Facilities pings you: the plants are almost dead.

options.text: Water them today and set a calendar reminder
Apologise and ask a colleague to cover this once
Treat it as too small to matter

title: You survive a round of cuts and inherit the work
situation: You go through the extra work with your manager: what you can carry, what needs more people or time, and why covering at this level should come with something in return. They like how organised you are and that you have taken it on, give you some support, and note your contribution. Covering becomes a way to prove your value.

options.text: Cover the critical work well, and turn “stepping up” into a case for promotion and a rise
Ease off after the conversation, and do not deliver what you promised

title: Colleagues invite you on a self-funded conference trip
situation: You still have not decided. Fares go up, and the organiser needs a final list. The group's keenness to have you along turns into mild exasperation.

options.text: Give a clear answer now, apologise, and accept the cost of dithering
Keep delaying until someone else decides for you

title: Mentoring a graduate who breaks things
situation: After you declined, Sam was given to Chris in the next team. Three months later Chris is seconded elsewhere, and Sam is behind on a client deliverable. Your manager calls you into a meeting room: 'You're the only person in the department who knows this area. You'll have to take over Sam's mentoring and help clear the backlog. There's nobody else.'

options.text: Take Sam on and help clear the backlog
Refuse again and say you do not have the capacity

title: A merge conflict wrecks release day
situation: The hotfix introduces a new conflict. CI goes red.

options.text: Stop the release completely and roll the merge back
Force the hotfix through

title: Whether to join a cross-team architecture review — and how hard to push
situation: The department tech committee is holding a cross-team architecture review next week, covering next-quarter rebuilds of several core services. Reviewers get a vote and share responsibility for the outcome later. You have been invited as a cross-team reviewer (you have a lot of experience with API performance and reliability). Accepting means three or four days reading their design docs and preparin

options.text: Accept, read the docs properly, and prepare comments
Decline and keep the time for your own team's delivery

title: A newly hired VP talks to you alone for ten minutes on day one
situation: The lunch lands. Chris finds out and warns you not to go over his head. Hale does not seek you out again either.

options.text: Apologise to Chris
Keep going round him

title: Whether to invest in a CI automation suite
situation: CI goes live and the team's merge speed improves markedly. New joiners find the configuration harder than expected, though, and the last two PRs sat blocked for hours. A senior colleague suggests loosening the gates so people can get used to the workflow, then tightening them later. You need to decide how strict CI should be.

options.text: Keep the strict gates and make the team meet the higher bar
Loosen the thresholds so the team can ease into the CI workflow

title: Grey-area items on a travel expense claim
situation: The claim goes through. Next month a spot audit flags your late-dinner line as 'possible non-compliance'. Finance asks you to explain or repay.

options.text: Repay it, admit you should have been stricter, and promise to stick to the policy
Say you followed team custom, and suggest Finance stop chasing individuals and set a clear rule

title: Mentoring a graduate who breaks things
situation: You took responsibility in public and Sam is hugely grateful. That afternoon your manager pulls you into a meeting room: 'We're already over our incident quota. Group wants a named person on the accountability report. If you keep this on yourself, the team can't carry it. I suggest you sign the draft that puts the main fault on Sam. I'll try to sort Sam's conversion to permanent another way.' They

options.text: Sign the draft and put the main fault on Sam
Rewrite it to match what happened: who skipped review, and which check in the process failed

title: An engagement survey that asks for your staff ID
situation: A month later Chris books a 1:1: “Someone said you’ve got an issue with me.” He does not know if it came from the survey.

options.text: Tell him face to face what you actually need
Deny it and say it may be a misunderstanding

title: You overhear a redundancy list that includes a friend
situation: Ethan screenshots your messages about the package. It leaks. You are called into a meeting with compliance.

options.text: Cooperate and explain exactly how it got out
Deny you told him

title: A database migration window clashes with peak trading
situation: You are leading the membership database migration from MySQL 5.7 to 8.0, scheduled for Sunday 02:00–06:00. On Friday, product announces that a peak trading period has been brought forward to Monday midnight. Chris, the DBA, says: 'The rollback script is not fully tested. Going ahead is a big risk.'

options.text: Ask to delay the migration and protect peak trading first
Cut testing short and go ahead as planned
Propose dual-write with a two-week canary cutover

title: A security hole that would be expensive to fix
situation: The release ships on time, and the temporary mitigations hold. Two weeks later monitoring shows access patterns that look like an attack, and the hole may already be in criminal hands. Security responds and confirms that a small amount of customer data was accessed improperly.

options.text: Open a full incident response: notify every affected customer and report it to the regulator
Scope the real impact, and recommend notifying only customers you can confirm were affected

title: Empty your savings for a deposit, or keep cash in case work goes wrong
situation: After months of looking you have found a flat that fits, but the deposit would almost empty your savings and the family's, and the mortgage would take a large slice of your pay. The industry is uncertain and your product line's prospects are not especially bright. Buying means years of heavy borrowing. Not buying may mean a long wait. What do you decide?

options.text: Do the sums: pick a mortgage you can live with and keep an emergency cash buffer
Go all in: empty your savings, borrow the maximum and bet your income will only rise
Hold off: build a safety net first and watch how your job and the sector go

title: Pushed on stage at the Christmas party
situation: You get up and run a quick game for the whole room. It goes down better than you expected. People are laughing, and your manager gives you a thumbs-up. Afterwards the host tries to keep you up there for the next part.

options.text: Quit while you are ahead: hand the stage back and return to your table
Ride the moment and keep hosting, even as you start to run out of steam

title: A new colleague with no sense of privacy
situation: Lou picks up on it, looks a bit embarrassed and stops. You move the conversation on to work and hobbies, and things feel normal again. A couple of days later she is asking about 'team gossip' again. She really does not seem to know where the line is.

options.text: Kindly suggest she gossips less and focuses on the work while she's new, for her own sake
Keep deflecting without spelling it out, and stay out of it

title: After dinner, karaoke with someone on the promotion panel
situation: The Lynx team dinner is over. Helen, the HR business partner, who sits on the promotion committee, suggests going on to karaoke. You have a headache and want to go home. Nine people have already signed up in the channel, and only you and Lee have not. Helen tags you: “Come on — no work talk, just singing.”

options.text: Go to the karaoke bar, keep your drinking in check, and join in
Decline politely and make sure you are sharp at the morning stand-up
Show your face for half an hour, then leave

title: A dependent team is late — do you escalate in the open?
situation: Once senior managers are involved, the other team is held to a hard deadline. Their tech lead tells you privately that 'there will be no more informal flexibility after this'. The working atmosphere sours.

options.text: Go to their tech lead, explain the escalation was about project risk, and try to repair the relationship
Accept the new way of working: formalise every dependency and drop the informal chasing

title: Pushed to sign a settlement agreement on the spot
situation: HR puts a settlement agreement in front of you and wants it signed today. Sign it and you waive claims you might otherwise bring. They say: 'Just get it done — better for everyone.' It is not binding unless you have had time to read it and taken independent legal advice.

options.text: Ask for time, take independent legal advice, and only sign a settlement you agree with
Sign the settlement today to get it over with, because you are tired of being chased
Lose your temper, tear up the paper and walk out

title: Pitching against a cheaper rival
situation: You run the rival down in the pitch. One of the panellists turns out to know them, and the room cools: “We asked for your proposal, not a review of someone else’s.” You look small, and it costs you marks.

options.text: Pull it back immediately and return to what your own proposal actually delivers
Keep going on about their past failures

title: A senior puts their name on an intern’s work
situation: Rowan says “it’s team output, we don’t divide it,” and refuses to change it. Quinn looks at you, disappointed.

options.text: Send the weekly update and the git history to your manager
Drop it

title: A former colleague at a competitor fishes for intel
situation: Felix pieces the merger together from other sources anyway. Helios goes after your clients with precisely targeted price cuts.

options.text: Tell compliance you may have overstepped the line
Stay silent

title: At the demo, your manager praises Product and not engineering
situation: At the sprint demo, your manager says the product design was excellent and does not mention the late nights engineering put in. The client is on the call.

options.text: After the demo, email the client (cc'd) with the technical highlights
Jump in on the call to explain how engineering built it
Say nothing

title: Another department’s major incident: do you volunteer?
situation: It takes seven straight days to restore the ledger. The CEO praises the payments team for showing up. The membership-benefits proposal slips and the client complains.

options.text: Ask your manager for extra people on the benefits proposal in return
Work late to catch up on the proposal yourself, without asking for anything

title: The company goes all-in on a new bet and sidelines your work
situation: You sit on the old product and bet the new direction will fail. The company keeps investing, progress is decent, and people and budget keep being pulled off the old work. You are a little more sidelined every week. Waiting is starting to cost you.

options.text: Stop waiting and push for a move onto the new work
Keep watching until there is nowhere left to go

title: Dependency upgrade breaks the build
situation: Dependabot auto-upgrades a transitive dependency and main goes red. You suspect a breaking patch.

options.text: Revert immediately, pin the version, and find the cause
Hack the code to match the new version
Disable Dependabot

title: The person next to you wears very strong perfume
situation: Your new neighbour wears very heavy perfume. A morning of it has given you a headache. She clearly loves it, and even asks, "Nice, isn't it?" Saying no might hurt her feelings, but putting up with it is miserable.

options.text: Tell her gently that strong scent gives you headaches, and ask if she could wear less
Praise it insincerely and keep sitting there with a headache
Turn to other colleagues and moan that she "stinks the place out"

title: A toxic team culture: stay or leave?
situation: The VP is furious. They start targeting you in public, handing you work that cannot be done, and hinting that failure will prove you are not up to your current grade. Other people start keeping their distance, worried about being associated with you.

options.text: Gather evidence and formally raise workplace bullying with the CEO and through a board channel
Faced with impossible work, ask for a lower grade or a transfer, and leave with some dignity intact

title: Your annual bonus falls short, and you go to your manager
situation: You skip the conversation and snipe in the channel. It reaches your manager quickly. You get no bonus correction, and you pick up a reputation for complaining behind people’s backs. A pay question that could have been sorted out has become a problem about you.

options.text: Limit the damage: take the posts down, apologise, and raise it through the proper channel
Keep complaining in public and make it bigger

title: A metrics problem, ten minutes before the briefing
situation: Your manager’s face tightens. They drop the slide and go with +12%. The VP asks why it is lower than the figure in last week’s comms. Afterwards your manager says: “Check this a day ahead next time.”

options.text: Offer to follow up with the VP on how the metric is defined
Leave it there so your manager is not made to look small

title: A newly hired VP talks to you alone for ten minutes on day one
situation: Two weeks later Hale does not follow up one-to-one. The gossip cools. Chris is back to normal.

options.text: Let your project results strengthen your position
Moan that it was a nine-day wonder

title: Escape room: your manager is slowing you down, a quiet colleague is flying
situation: You run out of time and finish last. The venue ranks you bottom. Chris says he was “not on it today.”

options.text: In the debrief, name Quinn’s contribution
Say nothing

title: A colleague accidentally posts internal architecture online
situation: They are grateful, take the post down, and become more careful about information security. Three months later someone else makes a worse mistake of the same kind: a log snippet containing sensitive customer data, picked up by an external crawler. Security's investigation finds that you knew about the first incident and did not report it, and they question your security awareness.

options.text: Admit you handled it badly, accept the company's sanction, and propose a 'good-faith warning' route for first minor incidents
Argue that the two incidents differed in severity, and that your call was reasonable in context

title: One conference place, and a question about Jo
situation: Your manager nods and says no more. Two days later the list is out: Jo is going. She thanks you in front of the team for 'putting in a word'. A week later she shares client leads from the conference, and your manager praises her in the team channel. You have to decide how you feel about it and what to do next.

options.text: Congratulate her and ask what she got out of it
Congratulate her in public, then tell your manager privately you want the next one

title: The new manager quietly moves you out of the inner circle
situation: You notice you have been quietly dropped from the core decision-making channel. A few important meetings no longer include you. Nobody has said it out loud.

options.text: Ask your manager where you stand and what is expected of you
Make your work so solid they cannot ignore you
Nurse the grievance, quietly check out and complain in private

title: Share options shrink in a buyback: living with the letdown
situation: Your grievance about the broken promises spills into your work. Output drops and you complain constantly. None of it brings the options back, and your manager starts to notice. Your performance slides too. Someone else made the mistake, and your prospects are paying for it. Time to stop the damage.

options.text: Set your feelings aside and decide: negotiate properly or leave, and stop sabotaging yourself
Keep coasting in protest and bet the company will not touch you

title: The client praises a feature you did not build
situation: The client is taken aback and asks for a contract annex stating that forecasting is not part of this phase. The remaining payment is delayed. Kim says you do not know how to talk to clients.

options.text: Help sales revise the annex and push a phase-two forecasting proof of concept
Stick to the accurate scope and stay out of the wrangling with sales

title: Neck pain with a deadline — whether to keep the physio appointment
situation: Delivery goes smoothly. At the weekend you get to physio, and while you are at it you buy a neck support and a sit-stand desk.

options.text: Use it as a prompt to change your habits, and set a timer to stand up
Once you feel better, go back to sitting all day

title: A metrics problem, ten minutes before the briefing
situation: The department’s quarterly review starts in ten minutes. You have just checked the Nebula Growth dashboard. Slide 7 of your manager’s pack says “MAU up 38% month on month”, but that figure mixes trial accounts in with paying users. The external definition counts paying MAU only, which gives +12%. These numbers are the highlight of the briefing. Your manager is making small talk with the VP and ask

options.text: Quietly point out the definition problem now and suggest correcting it in the room
Hold off for now and email privately after the meeting
Say nothing and let the briefing run
